speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne with some mixed emotions. My emotions are mixed by many things. They are mixed by the fact that this is the third speech I have written because over three months have transpired since the Speech from the Throne was delivered. I sympathize with the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette); he had the same difficulty, only he had to do it in three different stages.
Also my emotions are mixed by the government's record since April 14, the heat of July, the imminent return to our constituencies and families and our frustrations at both the lack of action, on the one hand, and the method of action, on the other.
It is my understanding that the Speech from the Throne is designed to outline the government's legislative program and what it will do, its philosophical attitude toward its term of office. Since my remarks provide me with an opportunity to review what the government has done, I should like to review the Speech from the Throne. 1 say to the member who spoke before me that when he commenced to address the Speech from the Throne, he indicated that he would review the great number of things his government had done since April 14. I took pen to paper and thought that I would make sure I did not miss anything. I made note of the $35 GIS increase, the $80 million to Petro-Canada, and then I stopped writing because that is all there was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You missed something.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the hon. member sticks around, he will not. In the original Speech from the Throne, His Excellency referred to the opportunity he had to visit the provincial capitals and the Northwest Territories during his first year of office. I make reference to that because of the fact he mentioned he was looking forward to visiting smaller communities across our vast and beautiful land. We in the riding of Simcoe North were pleased in June when he visited us. He has become a man of the people. He moves among the people very readily. He and his wife bring a grace and a presence, a warmth and a
The Address-Mr. Lewis
tradition of that office to the country of Canada. I am pleased to say that he is very, very well received in the country.
The Speech from the Throne referred to serious challenges. Canadians everywhere would agree that we face serious challenges, though we are fortunate enough to have great opportunities. The people of my riding will face those challenges in the 1980s as they have in the past. There is a determined resilience and an energy in my constituency and all of Canada to conquer the challenges of the eighties. The Speech from the Throne called for action. We commend the government's desire for that action.
Reference was made in the Speech from the Throne to the accumulation of essential legislation left from previous Parliaments. We were asked to dispatch that backlog expeditiously. It was suggested that the government is relying on the good will of members and senators of all parties. 1 was a new member during the last Parliament and I watched members opposite to see what good will was all about. I saw them debate the budget of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) of the fall of 1978 for 21 days during the fall of 1979 although it had not been changed. Where was that good will last fall? Where was that good will on the night of April 21 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) introduced a ways and means motion which was substantially what he condemned in December? Where was that good will when our party and the New Democratic Party were denied the traditional right to review that legislation? Sure, it was a ways and means motion, but Your Honour and I know it was legislation. Where was that good will?
I understand the Minister of Finance is suffering from a throat infection. It is no wonder, because that throat has had to swallow a lot of pride. If there was any good will left after April 21, it was blasted out of the water on July 11, which was a Friday, late in the week, when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) introduced his infamous tax on Canadian people. I know Mr. Speaker's background is that of a lawyer. There is a saying in the courts, "If you come to court demanding equity and justice, you must come with clean hands". I say to the government, "If you come to us relying on our good will, you must demonstrate good will yourselF'.
Reference has been made today and in the throne speech to the referendum in Quebec. On May 20 the people of Quebec went to the polls. Sixty per cent voted to remain a part of Canada and 40 per cent showed their dissatisfaction. I think 100 per cent deserve a better deal from this government. One hundred per cent of all Canadians deserve a better deal from the federal government.
I wonder where the Liberal party has been for the last 17 years. Why was this dissatisfaction on the part of Quebeckers allowed to reach the point where they challenged the federal government, which is controlled in all its aspects by an overwhelming Quebec Liberal caucus? That feeling of dissatisfaction pervades all provinces. Unrest is evident everywhere because there is a lack of understanding. We do not like the

July 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Lewis
method of negotiation, we do not like the province-bashing and we do not like the people who were sent to negotiate. Whatever the results of the referendum, we want to solve the problems. The government wants to anticipate them; we want to solve them with understanding. There are no winners and there are no losers when the constitution is debated. Canada and Canadians must be the winners.
It is my specific responsibility as a member of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to monitor, criticize and review the efforts of the minister of housing. In pious tones in the Speech from the Throne-one of the things that was missed in the list-it was stated that we are going to assist those unable to bear the burden of renegotiating their home mortgages in the present abnormal situation so that the spectre of foreclosure will be avoided. We know of no specific programs. We know of no specific help. And as the government said, the interest rates are coming down because the country faces a recession which this government is leading us into. We know that this government has accepted quit claims just as subway conductors accept transfers, as people abandon their homes leaving CMHC to resell them at prices that are lower than those of their neighbours who stay.
The Speech from the Throne said that we are going to encourage higher standards of home insulation. I commend the minister because that study has been made. I do not want hon. members to think that I am just picking the things that were not done. The study has been made, the study was necessary, and on this side of the House we look forward to receiving the results of that study.
The Speech from the Throne also talked about an improved Canadian home insulation program. Where is it? It is now July. We are coming to the month of August. It is insulation time but there is no program. There are no improvements.
I am pleased to see that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is in the House. In the Speech from the Throne there was reference made to the increased effort to develop critical trade skills. I would implore the minister to concentrate on that. We are faced with a double tragedy in Canada. We have a rapidly aging population of skilled tradesmen and we have young people out of work. We have to take action at all levels to curb this problem.
I know that the role of the federal government does not get into education; that is the responsibility of the provinces. However, there is a part for the federal government to play in co-ordinating the on-the-job training and the tax concessions that can be worked on. In my riding there are some very good people in the minister's department who go out to seek those opportunities. What we have to do is to push that program right across this country. There are link community projects which link the high schools and community colleges. The federal government and manpower department should be pushing that on-the-job training. It is vital to us because of the rapidly advancing average age of our skilled tradesmen.
In the Speech from the Throne it is suggested that the government will enter into a new partnership with voluntary agencies and local organizations in a program of community
service. This suggestion concerns me. People might ask why. In my opinion, the LIP grant mentality of the Liberal government over the past decade has eaten away at the morale of the volunteer segment of society.
Once upon a time Canadians performed a service to the community because they were concerned for humanity. There were worth-while community projects which Canadians accepted as part of their duty. Those programs are now being performed by civil servants, pseudo-civil servants and people working on grants. The government takes longer. It spends more and it destroys the will of Canadians to contribute to their communities. I urge this government to take a long, hard look at the volunteer sector of society. I suggest that we make it a partnership with a purpose and not a partnership by purchase.
Terry Fox is running across Canada to raise money for cancer research. He should become a symbol for Canadians to show what we can do in the volunteer sector of society. He is not working on a grant; he is working on a lot of determination, effort and concern. He is raising money by that dedication and concern. He will do it the way we used to do it before the federal government got into the business.
I wish to deal briefly with energy policy. I commend this government for recognizing that we need an energy policy in 1980. I will not talk about the 1970s or the 1960s when the government did not think we needed one. It has been suggested that a made-in-Canada price will solve everything. We think that the petroleum price auditing agency will act as a watchdog. There are a lot of questions to be asked. We are going to hold this government to an energy policy. Our party fought the last election on the basis that we were committed to one price for Canadians. We felt we should pay our way. We did not want to lay our deficits at the feet of our children and that meant an excise tax of 18 cents per gallon to pay for the courage of our convictions.
It has been suggested in the Speech from the Throne: "My ministers do not intend to impose an 18-cent increase in the excise tax on transportation fuels and the made-in-Canada price will result in a lower price to consumers than the one proposed in the budget of the previous administration." Those words are as infamous as the words "We will never impose wage and price controls."
The tax of 2.4 cents per gallon on heating oil will result in a higher tax for consumers than that proposed in the budget by our party. The tax of 2.4 cents per gallon is to permit the world price to be paid for tar sands energy. Not 85 per cent of world price, but world price. That is what we said we would never move toward.
I say that the Liberal party has cast adrift the Liberal candidate in my riding in the last election. He has had some problems. In 1974 in Scarborough West, Alan Martin said "We will never institute wage and price controls". In 1979 he went back to the same people. In 1980 he tried my riding and he said "The Liberals will not impose an 18-cent excise tax on transportation fuels". He did not say that it would be less, he did not say it would be more. He forgot all about home heating
July 17, 1980

oil. Ele said that the Liberals would ignore world price, and that was an ironclad guarantee. I said that Mr. Martin had been set aside and cast adrift by the Liberals, but really he has not. Ele has been awarded a contract through the ministry of energy. For 1 5 days' work he is paid $7,300. My pay, as a member of Parliament, for one year is $30,600.

speechtext: Tell the truth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let us talk about his expenses now. His expenses for 15 days are $10,300. My expenses for a year are $13,500. 1 am pleased to have that in the record.
This government promised to reduce the federal deficit in a planned and orderly manner. We want to know when that will start. What was denounced in December was clutched to the bosom of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in April as a drowning man reaches for a life raft. The deficit is larger. The planning is absent. We agree with the premise: Canadians want effective government, not necessarily less government. We feel they want it while they are still alive.
I want to deal briefly with our economic potential because I have touched on many other matters. On April 14 the government said that it would reduce the deficit. One week later the deficit went up from $11.5 billion to $14.1 billion.
There is another ray of hope in the Speech from the Throne; this government reaffirmed its commitment to increase Canada's over-all expenditures on research and development to 1.5 per cent of the value of the gross national product. Where was that commitment in 1973 when the rate was 1.01 per cent, in 1974 when it went down to .98 per cent, in 1975 when it went down to .97 per cent, in 1976 when it went down to .93 per cent, in 1977 when it went down to .92 per cent and in 1978 when they broke the barrier of .9 per cent and it went down to .8 per cent? We do not know to what depths it will plunge in 1979. The government must stop paying lip service to research and development and begin to do something about it.
In closing, I want to take issue with two direct references which are of a regional nature found in the Speech from the Throne. They disturb me greatly. First, the government suggested in the Speech from the Throne that members who represent the people of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have a responsibility to represent their constituents to the nation. It is then suggested that they have an extra responsibility in the present circumstances to represent the nation to their constituents.
In my opinion that is a direct insult to every member in this House from those provinces. As a member from Ontario, I take exception to those remarks in the Speech from the Throne. The root causes of western alienation, as I understand it, are in that kind of thinking which destroys good will, determines enemies and divides our country. We sat here in the Parliament of Canada listening to Liberal cabinet ministers and backbenchers finally representing the nation to their constituents because of the Quebec referendum.
The Address-Mr. Laniel
This remark in the Speech from the Throne is a cheap shot at the hon. members from Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia from both parties and I resent it. Those of us who make an effort, not by twinning, to know the members from those provinces know that they are men and women of good will and that they are conscious of the balance between representing their constituencies and representing their country. They do not need to be reminded in this insulting manner.
1 think that everybody should make an effort, not just from day to day but every day.
It has also been suggested that there are some problems in central Canada. In central Canada it is said that there are some who fear that the economic strength of this region is somehow slipping away, and this has led to envy and bitterness. If that feeling exists, it only exists among members of the Liberal party. As a Progressive Conservative from Ontario, I can tell this House that we do not fear for our economic strength. Sure, there are momentary concerns, but they are always surpassed by an inner strength and resilience which can be found in our province and which some of the members opposite will always envy.
We were a founding partner in confederation and we intend to be a continuing partner in confederation. We reject the envy and bitterness as the problems of lesser men and women. We have faith in our party, in the people of Ontario and Canada which rises above the fears expressed by the Liberal party. Do not worry about the people of Ontario; we are participating partners and dedicated to a strong, united Canada and always will be.
In closing, I would say, as was mentioned by the hon. member who preceded me, that it is time for all of us to think of our country first and our province second. Canada is one country. Let us close ranks and prove it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the throne speech debate was interrupted on May 12 last, a major event occurred in the Canadian political life, when a majority of Quebeckers voted against separatism advocated by the PQ party and against its vague project of sovereignty-association, expressing quite clearly their desire to remain in Canada, a Canada where each province will feel more at ease and will benefit from a fairer economic distribution.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it can truly be said that the referendum results have relieved the Canadian people, more especially in Quebec where the tensions among the various classes of society or within families had greatly increased during the referendum campaign. The recent public opinion poll made by the Quebec Employers' Council, of which I have a copy here and which appeared in the July 10 issue of La Presse, shows that the defeat of the separatist option of the Quebec government had a very positive effect in business

July 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Laniel
circles, judging by the satisfaction expressed by Quebec business leaders in that poll at the economic, social and political climate in the province.
Mr. Speaker, 93 per cent of the business leaders polled found the social climate good or acceptable in Quebec since the referendum, while 82 per cent feel the same about the economic climate and 78 per cent are optimistic as to the political climate. That is a significant improvement over a similar poll taken six months before, that is in January 1980, and over all such previous polls taken before 1976 as well. Now, the Quebec premier, Mr. Levesque, stated following this poll that it would be absurd, that it would be "the height of absurdity to relate the result of the referendum to the improvement in the psychological climate in the Quebec business community.
However, as Yvan Guay, a leader-writer in La Presse, wrote in the July 16 issue, the president of Devencore Realties, one of the largest real estate firms in Montreal, stated recently in an interview with a Gazette reporter that the No-victory in the referendum had given new impetus to construction work in Montreal. Also, the deputy-manager of investment services of A. E. Lepage Company stated that he had made more business deals in the four weeks immediately following the referendum than he had in the five previous months. And a great many other brokers with him, Mr. Speaker. I will not quote Mr. Gray's, in view of the harsh judgment on Mr. Levesque's biased analysis, but I agree with him when he states in the same article that social peace and political stability are two major factors of a healthy economic climate.
On the basis of these premises, while most Canadians and Quebeckers are anxious to see the current constitutional negotiations come to fast and concrete results, I should like to deal for a while with the present government's concern for the future of our economic development and, more specifically, for putting together a train of economic policies likely to create jobs, accelerate growth, ease regional imbalances and favour Canadian control over our economy, as mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I have been nonplussed by the negative critics voiced by several hon. members from the official opposition this week during the debate on the Progressive Conservative motion, who apparently failed to recognize that over the past four months, the government had shown its firm determination and ability to deal with the problems and avail itself of every possibility resulting from the current economic context, and who dared even deny the fact that we had already implemented some elements of a policy of economic development and industrial strategy.
Mr. Speaker, the planning and drafting of a comprehensive economic and industrial development strategy cannot be done without putting together all the elements of the problem if that is to be done responsibly. And it cannot be done without taking
into account the impact such a strategy may have on the orientation of the economy in coming years. So it is understandable that while they have defined all the basic elements of that strategy, as I mentioned earlier, the government should momentarily defer its announcement but you will readily admit that they have in the past four months given priority to that industrial development, job creation, economic growth and regional distribution.
A central factor in the government's initiative was the decision that led to the decision concerning the F-18A planes which is going to promote economic activity and bring about an industrial development of over $3 billion for all of Canada, spread out over various regions, and that will be particularly beneficial to Quebec. When the contract was signed the economic fallouts for Quebec were estimated at $1,573 billion, and as a result of the interest shown by Canadian and Quebec firms, the economic fallouts for both Quebec and the rest of Canada will probably, as we read in several press reports recently, be much greater.
That program, Mr. Speaker, could create up to 24,000 direct and indirect jobs across Canada. The purchase of the new fighter for the Canadian Forces is also a key element in the development of high technology industries like the electronics and aviation industries which will result in promotion of our high technology and allow it to face more effectively foreign competition in the 1980s while at the same time resulting in economic fallouts worth over $3 billion.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, this government's commitment to guarantee private sector loans to the Chrysler Corporation of Canada starting in 1982 for a total of $200 million. At the same time, in return, Chrysler promised to invest $1 billion in Canada during the next five years, in addition to its commitments with regard to job creation, future production and the purchase of parts in Canada.
Everyone knows, of course, that the North American automobile industry is currently going through hard times. The newspapers are full of articles on the subject. And the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) is personally involved in various connections with the industry; his recent visit to Washington, as well as his statements, prove that he is determined to ensure Canada a continued profitable participation in the automobile sector. 1 would much rather have heard the hon. member for Hamilton-Mountain (Mr. Deans), every time he intervened, encourage the minister in his efforts and actions, rather than try to see the mote in his brother's eye, inasmuch as our minister has proved his will to save jobs and his concern for Canadian workers. The same thing happened last week or the week before when I heard the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) put questions about to the inquiry undertaken by the RCMP into Space Research, as well as the subsidies or loans granted Valleyfield Chemical Products, a firm located in my riding.
July 17, 1980

Well, I would have preferred more positive questions than those asked by a member who simply wanted to know who the guilty party would be in this matter. We forget that, in subsidizing Space Research and in creating the Valleyfield Chemical Products Company, the federal government took over a business which employed 250 people, and that there are now about 650 employees on the company's payroll. For my part, 1 believe job conservation is more important and as 1 said, 1 would have preferred to hear hon. members urge the government to tidy up what might have been some loose ends in this organization or in these businesses or even with respect to its past, but to deal mainly with preserving these jobs.
Mr. Speaker, with respect to international trade, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has already had a dynamic influence on foreign markets by creating the position of Minister of State for Commerce and, since his return, the possibilities are limitless. The dynamic measures taken by this minister and the creation of an agency to deal with foreign trade will be of great help to exporters and enable the Canadian industry to sustain foreign competition more easily on international markets and on the Canadian market. Obviously, everyone in the House is aware of the views of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) on economic nationalism since he is the author of the famous report published some 10 years ago which called for more stringent measures to lessen the foreign stronghold on the Canadian economy, and led to the creation of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, FIRA. The government is severely criticized and some people ask for tighter legislation on foreign investment control, and yet they express doubt about the government's willingness concerning the amendments it intends to make to the Act.
During the last election campaign and in the Speech from the Throne, the government made known its intention to extend and reinforce FIRA's role, and the minister mentioned in his speech in the House on July 14 that he is contemplating submitting a series of measures to this effect which would reinforce the Canadian participation in the economy, improve the role of foreign companies in our economy. As a result of those prospective changes, Mr. Speaker, FIRA will have to publish before taking any decision the list of all major proposed take-overs which are under review, a procedure that the legislation does not authorize at present. The agency will also be authorized to undertake a periodic performance review of some Canadian branches of foreign corporations in key sectors such as research, development, high technology exports and so on. This is important.
I hope that the same companies will not always be the subject of such performance reviews but that they will be done in an orderly manner and will also deal with the small Canadian companies which can be branches of large international corporations. Those amendments will provide for some finan-
The Address-Mr. Laniel
cial assistance to Canadians who would like to compete against foreigners and purchase Canadian companies, or buy back the equity held by foreigners in Canadian corporations, or still purchase branches of foreign corporations which would become available.
We also heard last month the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), who was here earlier, announce certain new initiatives in the field of employment, and especially of training, which shows the concern of the government for an essential aspect of the approach we will have to take for the eighties in the area of human resources and manpower adaptation. In addition, the recent establishment of a special parliamentary committee, a task force on employment opportunities in the eighties, will enable the government to obtain the opinions of the greatest possible number of people concerned about future aspects of employment, and especially the needs in specialized fields.
Mr. Speaker, since energy is closely related to the industrial strategy, unlike the Progressive Conservatives who wanted to get rid of Petro-Canada, the government sees in this organization a tool for economic development, to develop our energy resources, and the very basis of our economic development if we also set a Canadian price for our oil. This week I heard certain western members complain about paying the same price as anyone else for consumer goods from the east and about paying the international price for certain products that westerners must buy, and claiming the right for the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the producer provinces, to receive the international price for their oil.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, 1 do not quite agree with all this. My colleague who spoke before me talked about Newfoundland and about the possibility for this province to understand the Canadian entity, the concept of sharing in Canada. As for me, I submit and everyone in this country must realize it, that the international price of oil is an inflated price which does not necessarily reflect production costs. I am prepared to accept the responsibilities of a policy that will ensure that all provinces will benefit from their natural resources, oil or whatever, in an equitable way. But it is through dialogue, through mutual understanding that we will be able to keep moving forward in Canada, while sharing at the same time.
Mr. Speaker, rather than submitting our economy through all the ups and downs created by international producers, we will be in a position with Petro-Canada, with a made-in-Canada price, to maintain our competitive edge on world markets, since our energy resources put us among the top industrialized nations. The new Canadian strategy for industrial development must clearly take into account the future potential of the western world economy, but also the current Canadian industrial structure and certain directions and alternatives that are now open to us on the economic level.

July 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Laniel
There is increasing reference to gradual liberalization of trade between most GATT members, which means for Canadian businessmen a significant opening of new markets in nearly one hundred nations across the world. During a meeting I attended this week, there was mention of textiles and someone suggested: In the United States things are going because they have a large market. Liberalization of trade will give us access to such a market if trade barriers are abolished. But if they are, there will be more pressure, especially in the weak industries.
Mr. Speaker, I think that even if we must accept stiffer competition on our domestic market, the government should assume its responsibility and protect its own economy. So, it is more than ever necessary to have a well structured economy to face this increasing competition from outside and this is why this government wants to play an active role in the economic situation of 1980.
If we had not purchased, as the Liberal government did, De Havilland and Canadair, I wonder what would have happened to the Canadian aeronautical industry and our country would have deprived itself of a high technology industry which allows most industrialized countries to compete on international markets and create highly specialized jobs. So we will continue to support actively the efforts of those two companies in particular, as well as those of other Canadian manufacturers and exporters, by giving them, through the Export Development Agency, government support like that given by Japan and many other countries to their exporting companies.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government is committed to support advanced technology industries on which our economy will depend even more in the coming years, but it is also necessary to maintain the hundreds of thousands of existing jobs in the automobile industry to which I referred earlier or other more vulnerable sectors such as textiles and footwear. I know that cabinet was supposed to make a decision today concerning the extension of quotas for footwear. Also, this week, the Textile Board has presented to the minister its report that will guide us in the evaluation of the future policies of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In those last two fields, while we should allow competition from developing countries, because we must share not only in Canada, access to the Canadian market should be regulated to maintain not only our jobs but also our productive capacity to produce Canadian goods specially designed for Canadian consumers by our Canadian technology which is growing more competitive in those sectors.
Some industrial sectors in foreign countries receive greater government aid because of increasingly stiffer competition and of the very high costs of automation of production, which leaves manufacturers with no other alternative than to amalgamate and seek government help. For an industrialized country like ours, it is of vital importance to maintain within our
territory, a production and research capacity in a variety of sectors whose products are part of the daily lives of Canadians.
This brings me to the topic of research and development, priority areas for the future in which this government wants to invest as much as other industrialized countries; it is seeking to increase investments in research and development from 0.9 per cent to 1.5 per cent of the gross national product. To achieve this goal, one of the means the government foresees is tighter control over the operations of multinational companies on our territory and, while still encouraging foreign investments, ensuring that these operations are consistent with present and future interests of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, coming back to the matter of Canada's political future, even though the results of the Quebec referendum helped restore a certain social, political and economic confidence, the problems of Canadian unity are apparent even in this House, despite the good will displayed by members, these problems which are also of an economic nature, are far from being solved. Faced with increasingly stiffer international competition, Canada must solve its domestic problems as soon as possible and form a common front to face its competitors. The provinces, the regions, do indeed have their own particular aspirations and claims, either in the field of energy, natural resources or whether they be of a cultural or linguistic nature, but that, Mr. Speaker, is the essence of our diversity. We must, however, transcend these differences as soon as possible to put the economic machinery back into high gear by taking into account our exceptional natural resources, our highly skilled and diversified manpower and develop an economic dynamism which would help us overcome our handicap because of the small size of our market compared to the vastness of our territory. This economic dynamism, Mr. Speaker, this confidence which is so essential for the progress of the Canadian economy is precisely the key to our future.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to be able to add a few final remarks to the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne this afternoon. In so doing I would like to talk a little about energy, about the pipeline, and I do so, of course, mainly from selfish motives, the main motive being that 450 miles of the Alaska highway gas pipeline will be eventually located in the constituency of Prince George-Peace River, that great part of our country which I have the distinct pleasure to represent in this House.
Much has been said about pipelines, both oil and gas, in recent weeks and months since we began this session of Parliament. One cannot speak about oil or gas, or about the Alaska highway gas pipeline, or the polar route or any of these energy schemes, without first projecting them against a global background. Today I particularly want to say something about economic nationalism and about nationalism in terms of energy politics.
July 17, 1980

When one looks at the global energy situation, in the period since the Second World War, if you lookback over the last 30 or 40 years, you will find that the statistics indicate that our demand on energy over the last 30 years doubled roughly every ten years. Indeed, comparing this statistic with the increase in the western world, at least, of the gross national product, one finds it is identical. In other words, gross national product in the western world increased or doubled every ten years. One can then make the correlation, or project ahead, by saying that the gross national product, or the improvement of the quality of life of western countries, will be directly related to the availability of energy in the future.
At the present time the total producibility of oil-and I am talking here exclusively about oil-is in the neighbourhood of 60 to 65 million barrels a day. We know, on the basis of projections which have been put together not only for the producing but also by the consuming countries and which are in the main quite accurate, that unless we can expect an increase in the total producibility of world oil of 1 per cent per year for the next five to eight years, and beyond that, we will have to begin to live with the situation where supplies of conventional sources of fossil fuels and energy sources will decline. Up to the year 2,000-in fact, after the year 1985- we must expect a decline beginning with 1 per cent per year and then accelerating at a much faster pace.
If we go back to the relationship with the gross national product, we find a very frightening picture, because we would have to accept the fact that the economies of the western world would no longer be able to grow. In fact the economies of the western world would inevitably decline if we continue to rely on the conventional methods of driving our industrial machine and sustaining our enviable lifestyle. It is a frightening picture as well, because many say that an economy of the type we have built for ourselves in the western world cannot survive unless there is an element of growth.
Many say that a business cannot survive unless there is an element of growth, an opportunity for people to progress within an organization. Indeed, many say that if our economies cannot survive at the present level and cannot grow, our political system is in jeopardy. And many say that this is a very important component of the oil politics which the east bloc countries and the Soviet Union are relying upon to destroy capitalism and the system of western democracy. That is basically the global picture.
If one now turns to the situation in North America, it is no secret that we in Canada and in the United States are using the lion's share of the world's energy resources. We are wasting more than we are using, of course, and we are criticized not only by our partners in the western world but, in the United Nations and other forums, by other nations which look upon us as irresponsible people who have little or no concern for the legitimate aspirations of people in other parts of the world.
If you look at North America you are confronted, first of all, with the demographic situation-260 million people on the North American continent; we in Canada number 23 or 24
The Address-Mr. Oberle
million. When we talk to our rich neighbours to the south, we are immediately confronted with their attempts to establish some kind of North American energy approach. We in Canada have, of course, always rejected that, because when it boils down to where the potential for future energy reserves lie, they lie in Canada. Since we number only 23 million people we should, of course, be very careful about how we share this energy, particularly with our friends to the south, but with other countries as well.
This is okay up to a point. But I want to portray a hypothetical situation, and this message is directed to my friends in the New Democratic Party, those great economic nationalists and energy nationalists. I want to portray a situation in the year 2000. Energy is extremely short and the world population has grown from four and a half billion to six billion people. Most of the new population is based in the Third World. They, of course, will have achieved a much better lifestyle and in so doing they will have placed incredible demands on the world's deliverability of oil and other energy resources, and the world is running out of fossil fuels. But we in Canada have been very prudent because in 1980, 1982, 1983 and 1985 we were very careful not to export any of our fossil reserves-gas, oil or anything else-to the United States or to any other country. So here we are.
The rest of the world machine has ground to a halt. People are freezing to death and sitting in the dark, but here we are in Canada with the lights shining brightly, our machines running at full tilt, and we are continuing this lifestyle which we have enjoyed and which our forefathers have built for us. Well, sir, I do not think that even my friends in the New Democratic Party are so naive as to think that that is actually possible and that we can actually totally isolate ourselves from the global situation of energy politics, and from the global situation of demographic politics, and sit here in Canada on top of all our wealth and enjoy it just for the benefit of ourselves and those who may come after us. The reality, as all of us know, is of course much different.
Instead of a continental energy policy we should be talking about continental energy co-operation. It is indeed against that background-I give credit to the former government, and 1 would even like to give a little credit to the present government-that some of the decisions that are relating to the most prominent project at the present time, the Alaska highway gas pipeline, have to be made.
We have to consider first of all that this particular project was planned to deliver gas which is exploited or harvested in Alaska to the lower 48 states. The Americans came to us in 1970 when the same question was raised in connection with delivering oil from Alaska to the United States. They came to us then as well, and told us that the most expedient, best, safest and cheapest way would be to run a pipeline through Alaska and through Canada, and to utilize as much as possible existing conduits and existing facilities to bring this important

July 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Oberle
resource down to their markets. At that time we procrastinated.
In fact much of the debate which has been going on here in recent days went on in 1970 and 1971 as well, when the Americans wanted to bring oil down. We in the west, and particularly I in northeastern British Columbia, never had any doubt that that was the proper route to take. 1 was selfishly motivated, of course, because I realize probably more than anyone what the economic benefits of that kind of system and that kind of industrial endeavour can be. However, at that time we frustrated the process so long that the Americans finally said that they could not wait forever. They were in dire need of this resource. They had to secure their own energy needs and to find some other alternative, and they did.
Alaska delivers to the United States roughly two million barrels of oil a day. The Americans built the Alyeska pipeline through Alaska, and facilities at the Pacific Ocean to load tankers to deliver that crucial resource down the west coast to the United States. As soon as the system was built, we went running down to the United States to say that we were worried about those tankers going down the west coast and that there could be accidents. We were worried that they could break up. They are vulnerable in a strategic sense. What if we ever got into a war with the Japanese? I hope it would not be with the Japanese, obviously, but the Russians might come and blow those tankers out of the water. What did we do?
The Americans frankly told us that they had asked us to build a pipeline through Canada but that we did not want that. Then we did not want tankers either. Here we are now in 1980, the Americans are now ready to deliver another 800,000 barrels of oil daily, and again the prospect of a pipeline is being discussed. Let us remember that 1,200,000 barrels are already proceeding by tanker, and again we are procrastinating. The Americans have really given up on us, and they are now building additional facilities to handle this additional oil. They are shipping that down by tanker as well, thus rendering our west coast very vulnerable in terms of the ecology and the environment.
That is some of the background to the pipeline politics in the west. That is another component of pipeline politics which is being considered as we make a decision on the Alaska highway gas pipeline.
The pipeline was always intended to serve the purpose of North American energy co-operation. There are some very significant industrial and economic benefits to Canada, but the pipeline is also planned to accommodate the delivery of our own gas from the Arctic to the south. All my friends have heard of the Dempster Link and the concept of building a pipeline from Inuvik to absorb the gas which is in the Beaufort Sea, and bringing it to the Alcan or the Alaska highway gas pipeline and joining it at Whitehorse, Yukon. The American line is so designed that it increases in size at Whitehorse and all the way down to the United States border to accommodate the delivery of our Canadian gas. Imagine, the Americans are prepared to pay the additional cost of increasing the size of the conduit to accommodate the delivery of our own gas. So it is
not just an American pipeline or a pipeline which is just in the American interest. There is a very clear Canadian interest connected with this pipeline as well.
The question of the pre-build is not a new concept with has been thrown in in the last three or four weeks. It was always talked about from the very beginning. It was always felt that it may well facilitate the financing of the whole scheme. We talk about $22 billion, $25 billion or $26 billion. Can anyone here really imagine the amount of money that is? It is money which is to be spent to a great extent in Canada. It is money which is to be spent to a great extent in Ontario, the industrial heartland of our country, where the pipe will be manufactured and where workers in the foundries will be making valves and other important components. In fact the Americans are really angry with us because they are totally out in the dark. Canadian firms have under-bid the Americans for the pipe every time, and the Americans are very angry. Imagine, one of the main components of the pipeline is of a size which the Americans cannot manufacture at all. It all has to be manufactured in Canada, and the Americans are saying that we are not fair.
American firms claim that we have too much of an advantage because of the difference in the dollar, but still the Americans have said "Let's go ahead". It is a competitive thing. After all, it is free enterprise. We want to get this project under way in the cheapest possible way, and as it happens Canada will get the lion's share of that $25 million that the project will cost.
It was always said right from the beginning, as I set out to say, that the pre-building of the line is almost essential to the financing of the whole. There never was any doubt that we have surplus gas in Canada which in the short term should be exported to the United States. Again I want to take hon. members back to the global picture and to this hypothetical situation I have explained. We have surplus gas. We have instructed our Energy Board to use a formula to ensure that over a certain period of time our energy needs are secure. The energy board is required, first of all, to look at the catalogue of proven reserves, identified reserves, and reserves ready for market, and to compare those with the demand which could possibly be placed on these reserves over a period of 25 years. In doing so the board is required to take a look not only at the present demand but also at the obvious necessity to convert major industries away from oil to natural gas and the obvious desire to extend pipeline systems to the maritimes and Quebec, to get away from reliance on foreign oil to generate electricity and to convert homes to natural gas.
Having taken all that into account, the National Energy Board is then required to protect all these needs over a period of 25 years. Anything that is surplus to that should be made available for export. Last year the Conservative government decided that at that time we had 3.75 trillion cubic feet of natural gas available for export. I should also say that the National Energy Board is required to adjust these figures from year to year. That takes us to the year 2005, and one does not
July 17, 1980

have to be much of a futurist to realize that the energy picture in the year 2005 will be quite different from what it is today.
When one looks around the world-and again we are babes in the woods-one finds that billions of dollars are being spent every year now on the research and development of more exotic forms of energy. The sun projects on the earth more energy in ten minutes than we have in our total fossil reserves. It is mind boggling to contemplate what that source of energy could do and will have to do in the future to sustain the lifestyle we now enjoy, and indeed enhance it, not only for ourselves but for Third World countries. One does not have to be much of an optimist to be optimistic about the future of energy. So I say that 25 years is a realistic and indeed a very optimistic time period in which to secure our energy future. In fact there is not a country in the world today, other than probably Mexico, Venezuela and some Middle Eastern countries, which has the luxury of being able to plan ahead for 25 years in an optimistic way.
Now I should like to speak about the concerns of the local area for which I have special responsibility. The situation in British Columbia is somewhat complicated and I intend, of course, to ask the government, once the decision with regard to the pre-build line has been made, how discussions with British Columbia are proceeding and their requirement for a statement of acquiescence with respect to the pipeline. At this point there is no agreement with the province of British Columbia on the final terms and conditions which will be attached not only to the pre-build leg of the pipeline but, what is more important, to the major portion of the pipeline of which 450 miles traverse northern British Columbia. Unfortunately, British Columbia has not been very aggressive or very active in participating or contributing to the study of the terms and conditions of the pipeline.
1 suppose it is for the first time that most of my colleagues here would hear of a report that was published about three weeks ago called "Forgotten Land, Forgotten People." It is the final study of socioeconomic conditions relating to this pipeline, a study which followed the Berger report on the Mackenzie valley, the Lysyk study with regard to the Alaska gas pipeline which was held in the Yukon. This particular study, which was conducted by Winston Mair, who was the inquiry commissioner, deals entirely with northeastern British Columbia. The title of the study "Forgotten Land, Forgotten People" is probably a little exaggerated, but it says something about the northern parts of our provinces.
We here in Ottawa have a more direct relationship with the territories because we still operate, to a certain extent, under a colonial system and we think of ourselves as colonial masters of the territories, something which I do not like and which has been challenged at least by my party on every occasion, and something about which we had very definite policies and plans. Nevertheless we know a little more about what goes on in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon than we do about what goes on in the provinces, because that is really their domain.
I have just published a report out of my own office which tells a little about the rip-off of northerners. I am not now
The Address-Mr. Oberle
straying away from the energy theme of my contribution today; I am just talking a little about the north because it is in the north that our energy future lies. In fact when we talk about the economic benefits which will be derived from the Alaska highway gas pipeline, the lion's share of these benefits will accrue to Canadians in all other parts of the country except the part where the pipeline will be located. In fact the economic benefits there will not be benefits at all; there will be horrendous problems associated with them. We are not strangers to massive projects such as that, particularly in northern British Columbia.
We have seen the construction of the Alaska highway itself and the construction of one of the largest hydroelectric projects, the Bennett dam, and we have experienced these kinds of industrial schemes where thousands of workmen are dumped into small communities which are already short of essential services. They impose their demands and needs on the area for short periods of time, and then they all go away while the local people are left holding the bag. Of course, we look with favour and excitement to the construction of the pipeline.
The report "Forgotten Land, Forgotten People" talks about the aspirations of the northerners in British Columbia in connection with this pipeline. It talks about the native people. In this case, while the natives have raised some questions that are as old as time, and some concerns about further assimilation and integration into the wage economy into which they are not ready to be assimilated or integrated, generally the natives in northeastern British Columbia also are excited and optimistic about the potential benefits which this project could offer them.
We have raised some legitimate concerns because while there are some real economic and industrial benefits which will accrue to all Canadians, any negative side effects of this project will be suffered only by the people who populate the land where the pipeline is located. Indeed, Mair accepted in his report many of the recommendations that I made in my submission to his hearings, namely, that we must develop a technique by which the amenities, the social services and the infrastructure in terms of transportation and communication and other things which might be required to accommodate not only the work force which will be building the pipeline but those who will be operating it in the future, must be paid for either by the proponents of the pipeline, or through some other scheme by the rest of the Canadian taxpayers who will, after all, receive the lion's share of the economic benefits.
I have proposed the imposition in northeastern British Columbia of a benefiting area tax which would tax the pipeline right away. The money which would accrue from such a taxation scheme would be used entirely to upgrade the transportation and communication infrastructure to help the small communities absorb the new work force which will be locating there permanently by providing them with sufficient means to build local services such as sewers, water, and even some recreational facilities, hospitals, and so on. The idea was certainly considered favourably by the government and recommended by the inquiry commissioner who was exposed for

July 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Oberle
some period of time to the realities of northeastern British Columbia. It has been a somewhat uphill battle to convince British Columbia to join in the scheme and to allow for a change so that the people in the north who sit on top of the energy will share on a fair and equitable basis in some of the benefits that will accrue.
Briefly I referred to the report published out of my office. If 1 may digress a little, I spent two years researching in order to point out, not only to my friends in the House of Commons but to all Canadians, some of the very real disadvantages which 5 per cent of Canadians living in 80 per cent of our land mass suffer as a result of the discriminatory tax regime in the country. I would encourage all my friends to read the report; it is available out of my office. In the report 1 pointed out that those 5 per cent of Canadians pay $470 million in unfair taxes every year. The report marks the beginning of a crusade I intend to take up over the next year in the north and in the south as well. It will encourage Canadians not only to remove the disparities, but to establish an equitable and fair system in the north to entice and encourage other Canadians, particularly young ones, to move away from the artificial, plastic and concrete environment of our cities, which are sustained by the resources of the north, to join in the excitement and the available opportunities of the north.
I notice I have reached the end of my time. I wanted to get that plug in because I am a little excited about this document. It may well be the most important thing I will do in my political career, particularly if my ideas are accepted by the government. Of course they are already accepted in the fact that federal public servants posted in isolation in the north are receiving very, very significant northern allowances and benefits which are not available to other northerners. 1 wanted to get this plug on the record today before the House recessed because I hope a lot will be heard about the report in the summer months.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This being the second Speech from the Throne to which I am exposed since becoming a member of the House, Mr. Speaker, I must confess that my reaction this time is quite different from the one I had when 1 heard the first one under a Progressive Conservative administration.
When I rose to deal for the first time with the address, 1 remember I was highly pessimistic, while this time around 1 am quite optimistic. A few minutes ago, as 1 was going over the notes for my speech of a few weeks ago, I came across my election pamphlet and realized that nearly all the promises which my party and I had made to my constituents of Shefford are part of the first Speech from the Throne, and that the local projects to which we had committed ourselves are being carried out just now.
While dealing with the Speech from the Throne, I think I can inform my constituents of the steps the government has taken and its attitude toward its commitments.
I think it is very important for us all to keep in mind what responsibility is all about and particularly for voters to realize that at a certain point in time politicians can make commitments and then keep them. I think that is probably going to be the trade mark of this Parliament and this government.
Like all my colleagues 1 would like to talk about the constitution because I think it is the vital element that is keeping us in active politics, particularly these years, and in commenting the result of the referendum I think my colleagues and 1 have all worked very hard to get a No-majority in Quebec, and I am thinking in particular of my colleague, the Hon. Jean Chretien, the Minister of Justice, who certainly managed to give all members from Quebec and several citizens of Quebec the desire to win. I think we should pay tribute to
July 17, 1980

him, and particularly for me it was an honour to work by his side. Now that the results are known, I think we should above all not take anything for granted but our leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in accordance with the commitments he also made at the time of the referendum, had promised to get intensive negotiations going.
I think the government agreed to meet its commitments toward Quebeckers. We are now witnessing a series of federal-provincial conferences and we realize that the will to change is not only in the speeches of politicians but in reality, and I think it is hoped that the provinces which are all sitting around the table these days, will want to co-operate with the federal government and allow it to deliver the goods to all Canadians, and Quebeckers in particular.
I think there is only one obstacle to that quest for renewal, and it is perhaps the presence at that table of PQ ministers who are acting every day like offended virgins and want to have us believe after the results of the referendum that they have become federalists and want to improve the federal system. I must admit that I am looking forward impatiently to an election in our province so that the Quebec negotiators sitting at that table will have that will of renewal and that openness of mind that will allow considerable improvement to this country, and particularly our constitution, to meet in an increasingly better way the aspirations of Canadians.
I think many had an opportunity to hear the speech of Miss Begin, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when she called for the participation of the people in the process of renewal. I think that participation by the people is essential because if Canadians do not have a means of expressing themselves in this constitutional renewal, if they do not have a channel to go to to voice their claims, I am afraid they are going to witness, as my colleague from Newfoundland suggested earlier, a cock-fight between federal and provincial politicians, and if the people are not in on it, it could be difficult for them to see through all those fights that are taking place around the tables and all those political wars.
So, as members of the Quebec Liberal caucus, we are striving to create a committee which could convey to the government and federal negotiators the considered opinion of the people-and when 1 say the "people", I mean it in the noblest sense of the word-the people who also want to have their say. 1 think that all those constitutional exercises should really aim to achieve a better administration of the affairs of State, but above all, to better serve the citizens.
I appeal to all of those who are involved in those negotiations to really keep that objective in mind, and perhaps to set aside, to a certain extent their self-interest or even, perhaps, in some cases, their thirst for power or a for a bigger share of the cake and to manage the country with greater concern for its citizens. If the federal government is better suited to deal with some areas of jurisdiction, by all means, let it keep it or even get it but, on the other hand, if provincial governments are
The Address-Mr. Lapierre
better equipped to deal with some other spheres of jurisdiction, then, well and good, let us hand them over to them; but above all, let us make sure that it will be for the benefit of the citizens and not for the glory of a some politicians. To pursue along the lines of our commitments, I think that especially in my constituency industrial development is one of the key aspects of the economy and, the fact that the Montreal area has been designated for the purposes of the DREE grants program is a great boon to our economy. All the new businesses in our area-there have been hundreds in the last few years-were set up largely through DREE grants and the fact that it has been decided to extend the program in the eastern townships region will allow us to create new jobs.
A little while ago I heard an hon. member say that the textile and rubber industries were very important in his riding and, these industries are considered important in mine as well but it is widely accepted that these industries must also be buttressed by other related industries or other high technology industries likely to provide workers with viable and profitable jobs in the area. I have in mind industries such as General Electric and that is why I was happy with the Canadian government's decision regarding the F-18, because the company involved has promised to build a plant in the eastern townships thereby creating some 650 jobs; it is very important for us that we should develop this new technology and the F-18 program will certainly provide for it and create new job opportunities for the young people coming out of the universities, the CEGEPs, etc.
I was particularly interested in the proposed grants for a $237 million contract to build military trucks; and I hope a decision will be made on this matter in the forthcoming months.
Mr. Speaker, the Bombardier company is located in my riding. It is keenly interested in this contract to build military trucks and would be ready to create new jobs in my area and, I think that the cabinet's gesture in asking Bombardier to make a bid for this important project is already most encouraging for us. You know, when the company's founder, Joseph-Armand Bombardier, started his snowmobile business, he thought it would be the vehicle of the future. Unfortunately, it has become a rather expensive recreational vehicle and the sales volume has not been increasing and in diversifying its production, Bombardier could include military trucks. Now, the advantage for us would not only be the Canadian contract for 2,800 trucks but the subsequent opportunities for exporting these trucks throughout the world and creating a viable industry in our area. That is why I am happy that we have asked Bombardier to make a bid and 1 hope the government will consider it favourably.
Another economic development project which is very important to us is the development of Mont Orford as an international tourist area. We know that DREE is negotiating with the Quebec government to include Mont Orford in the tourist

July 17, 1980
The Address-Mr. Lapierre
development area. You can be certain that 1 am trying very hard to give to that area of my riding a year round tourist industry which could also create permanent employment. Speaking of job creation, 1 was very pleased to publicize the announcement made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) about the $137 million program to create new jobs, particularly for development and community services projects.
Earlier, I heard a Progressive Conservative member criticize those programs that will allow us to create jobs and give work to people who want to work. If he does not want that money in his riding, we are going to take it. Maybe there is no unemployment in his riding? Very well, we will take that money! That type of program is very important to us and I protested against the disappearance of Canada Works Program that the Progressive Conservatives were going to abolish because it is important for us as well as for various organizations and our community. Senior citizens, the handicapped, all kinds of volunteer organizations have taken advantage of it and we want also to train our unemployed because, in an area like ours, young people have problems to find work and that kind of project will allow them not only to continue their search for a permanent and profitable job but also to gain a diversified experience while serving the public. I certainly prefer to see our young people and our unemployed work in those community projects rather than drawing unemployment insurance to stay at home. Idleness is the root of all evil and it might be true! The summer projects that have been announced made me very happy. Almost $150,000 have been spent in Shefford and if this is a waste for the Progressive Conservatives, for us it is indeed a good investment. During this summer, some 40 or 50 young people are trying to help their community thanks to those federal programs and this makes us very happy.
The maintaining of the employment tax credit is also very important to us. A number of firms have been and will be benefiting from the extension proposed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. And speaking of employment and immigration, I wish to mention something which is of particular interest to me, the in-depth review of the whole unemployment insurance program announced by the minister. As a member dealing with some 40 to 50 unemployment cases each week, I want to take an active part in that kind of review of the unemployment insurance rules because often, quite honestly, the complexity of the regulations and the lack of understanding displayed by some officials will discourage some unemployed, and will even have them feel they are almost treated like tramps. Often it is the result of an accident they suffered in their life. I know of persons who have been working for 30 and 40 years, who had to go on unemployment for all sorts of reasons, and I feel that the regulations should be, perhaps not eased up but simplified. It is therefore with much pleasure that I welcome the review and also, if I may, I would like to suggest to the government that people between 55 to 65
do not have enough programs tailored for them, although they have specific problems. We have established employment programs for the young, for women, for natives, for almost everybody but that group of workers. In my view, when someone loses his or her job at 55, it is very difficult for them to go and apply here and there. He or she may apply, but getting a job is another thing. This is a problem which will have to be tackled because in my area, especially in the textile industry, there have been numerous lay-offs. Right now many workers are at a loss. They can go on unemployment for 52 weeks but that only leads them to age 56. Then they face some problems. I therefore urge the government to look after that specific group of people because they have specific problems.
Over 65 years, there are senior citizens. I am therefore happy to see that we have honoured our commitment made in the Speech from the Throne by adding $35 guaranteed income to the supplement.
Many people in my constituency who will receive the supplement for July will benefit greatly from this initiative.
However, there is a sombre note in all this. The Quebec minister of social affairs has taken away $20 of these $35 for all senior citizens in nursing homes, and this same minister has had the gall, and it really takes a lot of gall to do this, to announce to the senior citizens that he was giving them an increase. At the same time, instead of giving them an increase, he is taking away $20 from them. 1 think that this should be pointed out to all senior citizens in nursing homes. The federal government decided that senior citizens needed $35 more, and the Quebec government appropriates these funds, for what purpose, I do not know, perhaps to pay for the referendum. It has appropriated part of the money that the federal government was giving to senior citizens.
As concerns housing for senior citizens, I believe that the minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is taking vigorous action to make up for the shortage of housing for older people. I hope we will all make more efforts to enable non-profit organizations to start building such housing or renovating senior citizens and low income housing.
With the rents at their present level, many senior citizens have a hard time finding proper housing. 1 believe we have an obligation in this matter, and many non-profit organizations are willing to contribute to building new housing, but unfortunately the funds are insufficient and I would certainly like to see, in the weeks and in the months ahead, additional funds earmarked for this program which, by the way, is much better than a direct government construction program because 1 would rather see volunteers getting involved in housing rather than some government officials and going through tender after tender because that always ends up costing twice as much as expected, whereas non-profit organizations can certainly play
July 17, 1980

a major role in building. As far as renovation is concerned, 1 am very happy to see that the government granted the major city in my riding $1,367,000 last week to upgrade the city core. This is a cost-sharing project where the federal government contributes 50 per cent, the province 25 per cent and the city 25 per cent. That is true co-operation between governments and that will help make downtown Granby a good place to be. I think everybody will benefit. Hopefully, this federal contribution will give Granby, which is called the princess city of the eastern townships, a greater role to play.
The throne speech spoke a great deal about energy. Rereading the election pamphlets I realized that most of our commitments are fulfilled. We promised Canadians that there would be no unfair 18 cent tax. To my knowledge, there is none. We promised Canadians to do our utmost to give them a made-in-Canada price for oil, and we are still doing our utmost to achieve this and we also want to set up an oil prices monitoring agency. I think that will come soon and I think it will help reassure Canadians who think that the large multinationals make excessive profits and charge too much. 1 think that is commendable, and the sooner the better. But those are all commitments we made during the campaign and we are living up to them and making them realities. There have been references to the increased role of Petro-Canada. I think that with the re-election of our party Petro-Canada can have no fear for its future because we believe that agency can play a most important role.
1 heard a member opposite talk about the metric system earlier. Several opposition members are complaining that the conversion to the metric system is not working in their area. Yet our area has been designated for metrication.
