speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 want to thank the House for giving me the opportunity to speak at this time on a subject that is of interest to this House and the country. I wish tonight to make a statement concerning the pre-build project of the Alaska pipeline. 1 wish to state from the start that the government has taken a decision to approve in principle the construction of the Alaska pipeline.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

In 1977, Canada and the United States signed a bilateral agreement for the construction of the gas pipeline. In 1978, legislation to implement the agreement was passed by Parliament. Since then, two important developments have altered circumstances. First, the estimated completion date for the pipeline was set back from January, 1983, to the end of 1985.
Alaska Gas Pipeline

There has been, therefore, a delay in the original time for the scheduled completion of the line from 1983 to 1985.
The second major change relates to the proposed pre-building of the southern segments of the system. Its initial purpose of exporting Alberta gas to western and mid-western U.S. markets has taken on considerably greater importance. Prebuilding has become of prime importance in two ways: first, as a means of facilitating the completion of the entire project; and, second, in terms of the substantial and widespread economic benefits it promises to provide Canada.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 am sorry if some members of the New Democratic Party are feeling sick. I am sure there must be a doctor in the lobby to take care of them.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Why don't they just walk out like they did the last time?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
In its original conception, as indicated, the southern portion of the line was to be built only moderately in advance of the remainder of the system in the north. The effect of the delays I mentioned has been the pre-building can now take place well in advance of construction of the rest of the system.
There has, of course, been another development. In the intervening years the volume of Canadian gas surplus to our needs and available for export has grown from some 800 billion cubic feet to around 4.5 trillion cubic feet. A number of steps have been taken by the government to take this changing situation into account.
First, the National Energy Board made the following determination: if pre-building were to be undertaken on schedule, with commencement of the construction of the western leg this summer, then it would be necessary to modify condition 12 of the Northern Pipeline Act. Because of the delays which I mentioned it would have been quite impossible for Foothills (Yukon) in these very different circumstances to meet the original requirement of establishing that financing had been obtained for the whole line in Canada.
Second, on April 2, the National Energy Board issued an order amending condition 12, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. The amendment required Foothills to satisfy both the Board and the minister responsible for the Northern Pipeline Agency on two major points. First, they had to be satisfied by Foothills that financing had been obtained for pre-building of the southern segments of the system in Canada. In the second place, they had to be satisfied that financing could be obtained for the remainder of the system before construction of the pre-build would be authorized.

July 17, 1980
Alaska Gas Pipeline
Third, also on April 2, Senator Olson requested the NEB to hold public hearings in order to obtain evidence as to whether Foothills could meet the terms of condition 12 as revised with respect to financing. At the same time, however, he advised the Board that the government intended to defer consideration of its order on this condition until it could also consider two other closely related matters. One was the pending recommendation of the NEB with respect to applications from Pan-Alberta. The latter had requested a licence to export an additional 500 bcf of gas remaining in the unallocated surplus previously identified by the board as a means of establishing the financial viability of the pre-build.
The other matter requiring consideration was the position of the United States government-its view as to the financeabili-ty of the pipeline system within its territory and the outlook for its timely completion.
Let me deal with the last issue first. The government has before it information on a number of steps which have been taken in the United States to encourage and facilitate the commencement and expeditious completion of the project by late 1985. These steps include recent decisions by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission certifying the pre-building of the western and eastern legs of the system in the lower 48 states for the initial purpose of transporting surplus Alberta gas pending the through-put of Alaskan reserves. They include also the June 19 agreement between the major gas producers in Alaska-Exxon, BP, Sohio and Arco-and Northwest Alaskan, the pipeline sponsor in that area, on the sharing of some $500 million in expenditures to complete final design and engineering work required to construct the pipeline and conditioning plant in Alaska, and to arrive at final cost estimates. On June 19 the producers and sponsor also signed a statement of intention in which they undertook to work together to facilitate the financing of the pipeline and conditioning plant in Alaska with a view to achieving completion of the system by 1985.
As hon. members are all aware, the strong and continuing commitment of the U.S. Congress was forcefully expressed through a joint resolution unanimously approved by both Blouses within the past few days. This resolution emphasized the conviction of Congress that the Alaska pipeline remains- and I quote-"an essential part of securing this nation's energy future and, as such, enjoys the highest level of congressional support for its expeditious construction and completion by the end of 1985."

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: I might say that this resolution was passed by Congress at the urging of the Canadian government represented by Senator Olson in those discussions.

Based on all these factors, and on the formal assurances which President Carter has today provided in a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Canadian government is prepared to accept the U.S. government's judgment that the project within its territory can be financed and will be completed expeditiously.

I apologize for the fact that the president's letter has not yet been translated into French-it has only just been received-but the other documents are in the two official languages.
Based on all these factors and on the formal assurance that President Carter has provided today, again, the government has accepted the United States' commitment assuring timely completion of the whole project. I repeat-timely completion of the whole project.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
The government is also prepared to authorize additional exports recommended by the National Energy Board through the pre-build system in order to establish the financial viability of that stage of the project. It also approves the amendment to condition 12 made by the Board.
Madam Speaker, 1 referred earlier to the hearings undertaken by the National Energy Board on the ability of Foothills to meet the revised condition 12. In a statement following these hearings, the NEB raised four matters of concern with respect to the financeability of the project in Canada. All these matters related to issues involving decisions made in the United States. Foothills itself initially raised all these issues as being potential problem areas. However, in response to an inquiry on this matter by the NEB, Foothills indicated that because of more recent developments it was confident that these issues had been, or would be, satisfactorily resolved.
However, it still remains necessary for the Board, and Senator Olson, to make a judgment as to whether Foothills is, in fact, capable of meeting the requirements of condition 12, as amended, with respect to the financing of the project in Canada. I expect that both the Board and Senator Olson will be in a position to reach a decision on that question within the next few days. Assuming this last issue of policy is satisfactorily resolved, the way will finally be cleared for a start on construction of the Alaska highway gas pipeline. The southern segment will commence within the next month.
July 17, 1980

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
It has been suggested in some quarters that the pre-build would amount to the construction only of an export line and represent a very different project than that provided for in the Northern Pipeline Act. Such an allegation is completely groundless. What is proposed is the construction, in two stages, of a fully integrated system capable of carrying Alaska gas to the lower 48 states and providing access to Canada's own gas in the Mackenzie Delta.
1 spoke earlier of assurances by the United States government. We are satisfied that the United States Congress and the United States administration are fully committed to building their portion of the line by 1985. We base this not only on the assurances already received but on a recognition of the absolutely vital national interest of the United States in gaining access to its gas at Prudhoe Bay, which represents more than 10 per cent of all its established reserves and its largest single new source of energy for the foreseeable future.
First, as I stated earlier, construction of the southern segments for the initial transportation of Alberta gas would spur completion of the entire project. It would provide an early cash flow to pipeline sponsors which would be a big help to them in financing the remainder of the pipeline.
Second, by stretching out the construction timetable it would also ease the strain on skilled manpower and the supply of goods and services, and ensure a very high level of Canadian input into the project. In other words, the pre-build fits in with the current economic cycle of the country.
Finally, pre-building of the western and eastern legs and the initial export of surplus Canadian gas will provide substantial economic benefit to this country. According to estimates, this will result in direct capital expenditures in Canada of a total of $1.6 billion, the benefits of which would be felt right across the country in terms of jobs and output.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Of this amount some $655 million would be spent on the pre-build facilities themselves and another $935 million on installation of the production wells, conditioning plants, and the gathering and other facilities required to deliver the gas to the Foothills pipeline. The pre-build project and associated developments would create employment directly and indirectly over the period between 1980 and 1984 of 150,000 man-years.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
A substantial portion of those benefits will come through the potential sale over the life of approved export contracts of around $17 billion worth of gas and natural gas liquid byproducts, which in turn will provide a positive boost to Canada's balance of payments position of some $2 billion a year.
The export of natural gas through the pre-build will provide a substantial benefit to hundreds of small and medium-sized Canadian-owned producers, many of whom at present have substantial shut-in reserves because of the absence of markets either in Canada or in the United States. The opening up of markets for these supplies which are surplus to Canadian needs will provide the cash flows such producers require in order to maintain exploration at the high level required to develop additional reserves with which to meet our own requirements over the long haul. For some of these Canadian companies at least, a failure to secure early access to U.S. markets could leave them with little choice but to sell out their interests to large multinational oil companies which can afford to hold gas in the ground for a long time. Such an alternative would clearly be contrary to our policy of greatly increasing domestic ownership and control of the petroleum industry in this country.
The pre-build, though, is just a part of the story. The total project, both northern and southern portions, according to best estimates, will in and of itself result in a 1 per cent gain in Canada's gross national product, with benefits including $2 billion in pipe orders to Canadian mills, 350,000 direct and indirect man-years of employment for Canadians, and the development of Canadian expertise and export capability.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Given the nature of the U.S. assurances and given the very substantial benefits which pre-building will provide-for example, facilitating the completion of the entire project and immediate returns to Canada in terms of jobs, output, producer revenues and balance of payment inflows-I do not believe that there can be any doubt that our national interest lies in proceeding with this important undertaking at the earliest possible date.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
The government has been considering this matter at length these last few weeks and took a whole series of measures to make sure that the whole pipeline would be built in the coming years and particularly by 1985. Today the American administration provided us with the final necessary assurances to convince us of the United States commitment to complete the proposed Alaska gas pipeline by 1985. From the immediate construction of the southern section of the Alaska pipeline will flow enormous benefits for the whole Canadian economy, not only for Alberta oil producers and the Alberta government, but also for manufacturers and particularly workers in each and every province of Canada, especially those involved in the steel and pipeline equipment industries. The construction now of the southern section is just part of the process toward the construction of the entire system of the Alaska pipeline that for the most part runs through Canada. The pre-build section will enable us to spread over several years the work and revenues necessary to build this pipeline. This project, on top of the one we have already announced regarding the extension of the gas pipeline to eastern Canada, particularly as far as Quebec City for the time being, will give a tremendous shot in the arm to the Canadian economy, in eastern as well as in western Canada, and that is the main reason that made the government come today to this decision which, I am sure, will benefit all Canadians.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have never in my time here seen nor heard a triple flip-flop such as the one I have observed tonight.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
We heard a minister just now make a statement, a minister who was a member of the government in 1977 and 1978, and who was in office when the Northern Pipeline Act was passed, which act required the construction of a pipeline. During the debate a discussion arose with respect to the pre-build and the necessity of that pre-build to finance the whole. The same minister in opposition made statements of which I am going to remind him in a moment or two because he has fallen far short, in his statement today, of coming up with those ironclad commitments of which he spoke last December.
Now he has flopped again-a flip-flop-flip. He is now on the side of the virtuous in reverting to the position of his government in 1977-78. It is a magnificent performance, Madam Speaker, a magnificent act. He really should, this ironclad man, be attending the Olympics as an acrobat.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: A trampoline artist.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Yes, a trampoline artist. Seriously, I have to reserve at least two positions here. One is a very serious one with respect to the amendments to section 12 of the conditions set out in schedule III of the act. There is no way that we on this side can exercise a value judgment as to whether or not the changes which are being made to section 12 are intra vires and are legal until we see those changes. They have not been made available to us, although I do thank the minister for instructing his office to make available to me at 15 minutes to eight o'clock this evening a copy of the statement he intended to make. Unfortunately, there were no copies of the president's letter attached to that statement, nor were there any copies of the changes to section 12 attached to the copy of the statement
Alaska Gas Pipeline
which I received, so we are unable to comment on these two very vital aspects of the minister's statement.
The reservation that I want to make-and I have not yet received copies, although I have requested them from the Table-is the so-called commitment of which the minister spoke in his statement, made by way of the letter which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) received from President Carter today. We must see that letter, and we must see the changes in condition 12.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: We should have a copy.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: As my friend, the hon. member for Northumb-erland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) says, we should have had a copy. That has been the weakness of the NDP position all along. They have been trying to judge this matter on the basis of an hypothesis. Always there was an "if'-if the government changes condition 12, will they not agree that it would be illegal to do so without debate? We do not know until we see the extent to which the government intends to change condition 12, and we do not know until we can make a value judgment on the legality of those changes. But their position is even worse than that. In 1977 and 1978 the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was their spokesman on energy matters. Madam Speaker will recall that he is now one of the officers of Husky Oil, I believe it is.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: They then took the position-and if there could be any act that exceeds the act of the minister in the art of the flip-flop-flip, it is that party over there.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: They took the position in 1977 and 1978 that there will be no pipeline. Also their position is very clear that there will be no exports of gas. Now they are trying to have us believe that they are opposed to the pre-build but they are favourable to the pipeline. That is one flip-flop. "But if you can assure us that the guarantees are there that the whole line will be built-I am still not going to let you put any gas through it because that is not in accordance with our policy- go ahead", they say.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION

They say, "No pre-build, but if the guarantees are there, we will change our position of 1977-78 as long as you build the whole gas pipeline. But for God's sake, don't put any gas through that gas pipeline". What act can exceed that kind of position?
There have been no changes in substance between now and last December when the minister spoke on an announcement made by the then minister of energy, mines and resources which is almost on all fours with the announcement made tonight. The only difference is that instead of 4.5 trillion cubic feet that we are being authorized to export, the figure was 3.7.

At that time the now minister had some very startling things to say. But I point out that apart from the letter from President Carter, which I have not yet seen, there have been no substantive changes between the position of last December 6 and the position today, not one.

What he is trying to do in his own inimitable convoluted way is to try to justify his own swallowing of himself and his words of last December.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: What a mouthful, that would be impossible.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said, it would almost be physically impossible. 1 really do not see how he can get past his iron head.
Condition 12 indicates that they have to be satisfied that the financing requirements for the whole line have been met. Now obviously that has been altered. It would be interesting to see just how it has been altered. Last December the minister made six conditions. The minister makes a moue, 1 will read those conditions to him to refresh his memory. In response to the minister's announcement on that date, he said:
I think this statement will be one that Canada will live to regret-
Essentially it was the same statement as the one made tonight. He continued:
-as one of the greatest sellouts we have seen.
That was the minister's value judgment on December 6 of last year as reported at page 2100 of Hansard for that year. He said that we should assume six points to be necessary prerequisites prior to the approval of the export and of the pre-build. He certainly laid his party's reputation on the line when he was making that statement speaking on his party's behalf. As reported at page 2101 of Hansard, he said:
-we are faced with the situation where eastern Canada, the Atlantic provinces, need more natural gas and need a gas pipeline to take gas to the homes and to the industries there.
I ask the minister to respond to this when he is replying to questions. Is it still the Liberal party's position that extension of the Q & M Pipe Lines to the maritimes must come before the pre-build which he has just announced, because that was his position of last December? Referring to page 2101 of the same issue of Hansard, he imposed a second condition. He said:
-with regard to revenues arising out of gas exports to the United States. They should be used to ensure the initiation and completion of the Quebec and maritime gas pipelines-
That is what he said last December, a few short months ago. Let me put this question to him: Is it still the government's position that revenues from gas exports to the United States be used to construct the full Q & M Pipe Lines? Are these government or private sector revenues that will be used to construct this eastern Canadian pipeline? That was his position and the position of his party when he was spokesman last December. He set forth a third condition then. As reported on the same page of Hansard, he said:
-we have an announcement that we will sell 3.7 trillion cubic feet of gas to the United States. That certainly is a clear indication that this government has its priorities all wrong.
Later on the same page he said:
Therefore, if we have to have a bias, our bias as Canadians should be against any gas exports outside Canada . . . That should take place only on the basis of an overriding national interest-
The factors, the elements and the circumstances have not changed in the interim between last December and now. What has changed? I ask Madam Speaker what has changed since December 6 except that presently the now government wants to export more than 3.7 trillion cubic feet? Or, does the government agree with its socialist friends to my left, their position that we should build a pipeline and not put any gas through it at all? If there is to be any logic in what the minister said last December, that has to be the compelling result of that logic.
He laid down a fourth condition then which is very interesting. Referring to the same page of Hansard, he said:
-there must be an arrangement for swaps in this agreement with the United States so that down the line, if Canada were to need natural gas, we would be in a position to obtain natural gas from the Alaska gas pipeline which we might need in exchange for the gas we are now providing to the Americans.
That was a very clear statement of his party's policies on the question of swaps which he does not mention at all in his statement tonight. I do not know whether it is an ironclad flop or whether he has increased his dexterity to a flip-flop, flip-flop, because he has already done it three times here.
I know that my harkening back to the rather rash statements which the minister made last December are certainly not comfortable to him, but it seems to me that they should be exposed in the light of the need for Canadians to assess the integrity of the kind of party that now sits there and .then sat here.
With respect to the fifth condition, Madam Speaker, that was imposed-and in this connection I refer to page 2101 of Hansard of December 6, 1979:
In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all-
-and the minister will remember the following words vividly. The sentence continues:
-an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline.
July 17, 1980

He went on to say that he was not satisfied with that firmness of statement, although the word "ironclad" cannot sound any firmer, but he went on to say:
Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered-before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.

In any event, Madam Speaker, so much for the president's letter which has been read by my friend. There is nothing approaching a commitment, the nature of which was contemplated by the minister, when he spoke last December.
Alaska Gas Pipeline
Regarding financial commitments, he went on at page 2102 of Hansard for December 6, 1979, to say this:
-we should have a commitment from the U.S. government in this respect, as well as from private industry.
I suggest to the minister that it would be stretching the truth beyond all recognition for him to even leave the inference that there is any financial commitment for the construction of the whole line. The conditions set forth in schedule 3, namely condition 12, make it abundantly clear that the minister-that is the Senator in the other place-must be satisfied that the financing is available for the construction of the whole line and not just part of it.
One thing which the minister did not touch upon, and he will recall that last December when the minister then made the announcement on December 6 of a seven-year time span over which the export would run, and he said-he, the minister now-at page 2102 of Hansard the following:
Our preference . . . has been for five-year agreements on exports. We are surprised that the government has been considering seven-year agreements.
He might address himself to that matter when he is replying to questions. Those are the views, Madam Speaker, which the minister expressed last December when he was out of office. Now he has suddenly become responsible again in the swallowing of himself.

The last ten minutes or so of the minister's 30-odd minutes' statement dealt with economic benefits. They

have always been there. Those economic benefits were spelled out when the act was before Parliament and before committee, and there have been no changes in circumstances whatsoever. 1 do not know what has taken the government so long in their shilly-shallying, delaying and fumbling in coming up with this decision.
I have one more point to which I want to address myself. It has to do with the response of the Prime Minister today when he was being questioned by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis), and I am referring to commitments that were given by Mr. Schlesinger. My friend from Perth asked him to table the current assurances and the Schlesigner commitment of some months ago in order that the House may see what differences, if any, are contained in the United States commitments. The Prime Minister must have been in receipt of that letter from President Carter when that question was answered. We did not have any tabling of that letter this afternoon in response.
More seriously, the Prime Minister in responding to the first part of the question said that, "on the Schlesinger commitment 1 think I made it clear at the time that the then secretary, Schlesinger, had told me verbally that we would not be wise to proceed with the pre-build if we did not have guarantees that the whole line would be built. So, I cannot table anything."
But last December 7 when the Prime Minister led the questioning for that day, he questioned the then prime minister, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), and he said this at page 2123 of Hansard:
Could I remind the hon. gentleman that our government obtained from the United States a commitment that if there were to be any pre-build of the Alaska gas pipeline, it could only be authorized if there were a commitment to build the entire line? Could I hear from the Prime Minister whether that commitment obtained from Mr. Schlesinger last March still stands?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that commitment stands.
The present Prime Minister said later on in his second question:
This phrase obviously indicates that there is no firm commitment, that we are asking them for a firm commitment and that we have authorized the export before obtaining this commitment.
We want to compare that statement of the present Prime Minister with the lack of any commitments, I am informed by my friend, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, who has read the letter, or anything approaching a commitment in the letter from President Carter. The decision to go ahead is bound to result in immeasurable economic benefits to this country. We have always been of that view.
However, the government has fallen far short of obtaining that degree of commitment to the construction of the whole line which the minister certainly expressed, in no uncertain terms last December, and which when they were in office previous to the last administration, they expressed just as strongly. They have fallen far short of obtaining the kind of commitment which will ensure the completion of the whole line. I very much doubt whether the time-frame of 1985 will be met. Indeed, when I took part in the debate in 1978, I
forecasted then delays which I anticipated would go to 1985 and beyond. From what I have heard tonight, those doubts have not only not been allayed, but my conviction has been firmed, that we are looking at a considerable piece beyond 1985 before we can see the construction of the whole line, indeed, if we see it at all.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on behalf of our party to speak on this issue which I regard as the most important issue of this Parliament so far. The minister during his speech looked across the floor and yelled at us on this side of the House words to the effect, "Do you guys feel sick or something?" Well, I do feel sick tonight.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: You look it.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: It is unbelievable that it is the same minister who is sitting across the floor tonight when one year ago, while he was in opposition and was the Liberal energy critic, he said | that the pre-build would be one of the greatest sell-outs in Canadian history. Tonight he has turned around and made a statement which is exactly the opposite. What makes me really sick is that the statement is sheer hypocrisy. Those are our feelings toward his statement tonight.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Tough luck.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
I would like to set out briefly and summarize I the position of our party because, unlike my friends to the right, I think it is very, very clear. What we have tonight is not a decision to build a pipeline, but a decision to export more Canadian gas which we think should stay in Canada to meet Canada's future needs.
There is no firm guarantee, none at all, that the rest of the pipeline will ever be built. The only thing which is guaranteed is that the United States will get our gas. Clearly, the government has failed to stand up for our interests. It has failed to get the ironclad guarantees which the minister so properly demanded when he was in opposition. The minister has failed to get the guarantees which would ensure the financing for the whole line. He has failed to get any swap agreements so that when we sell out the Canadian gas we receive, later, gas to replace it at the same prices from the Americans. The minister has failed to get that guarantee.
When I saw the minister receive a standing ovation for his speech of sheer hypocrisy, I wondered how the members opposite will go back to their ridings and say to their constituents, "Well, you have to pay more for gas in the future, because we are selling it all out now." In 1978 Parliament authorized a transportation pipeline to help the Americans transport Alaska natural gas from Prudhoe Bay through Canada down to the lower 48. What benefits were we to receive? We were to receive some jobs, to receive some contracts and so on for helping the Americans. We also were to receive a link up to the Arctic gas through the Dempster lateral. That is why Parliament passed the Northern Pipeline Act.
July 17, 1980

However, it was an act to transport American gas to American markets. Now, the government, without parliamentary approval or debate-and we have sought a special debate to have the matter brought before the House to find out about the guarantees-the government comes forward tonight, by order in council behind closed doors and against the real intent of an act of Parliament, brings in this announcement. It is clear to me, if it is not clear to the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), that the government has brought in an order in council which will authorize an export pipeline to export huge quantities of Alberta gas, Canadian gas to American markets. We on this side of the House say that this is a sell-out. Let us call it what it is. It is a sell-out of relatively cheap Canadian gas. Later Canadian consumers will have to pay higher prices, if we can get the gas. There is no guarantee that the whole pipeline will ever be build.
Some hon. members have raised in the House the fact that, according to the Prime Minister, even the Americans said that we would be damn fools to go ahead with the pre-build. Yet the minister receives a standing ovation for going ahead with the pre-build. That is what the Liberals think. I have never been more proud than tonight that I am not a Liberal.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
The minister, when he was the energy critic in opposition of course said, and the hon. member for Yukon gave us the words-they are familiar to this House-"Let us not sell out for a fast buck, let's have ironclad guarantees." Tonight the minister went against that statement totally. Not only has he flip-flopped, but he has given up the whole basis of his energy policy. As I recall, the minister's energy policy is to get Canada off oil. That part of his policy makes sense to me. Does it not make sense to use cheap Canadian natural gas to replace that expensive imported oil? That is a good policy and one with which I agree.
The problem is that when Ontario, Quebec and the other eastern provinces are ready to convert, they will ask, "Where is the gas?" It will all have been sold to the United States by this pre-build. I draw to the minister and hon. member's attention the Liberal party policy of 1980 which reads at section 124(a):
As far as practicable, a distribution network should ensure that all regions of Canada are linked to the provinces rich in energy resources.
It goes on to say in subparagraph (b):
Exports of energy or energy sources should be very carefully assessed to guarantee Canada's long-term interests.
There goes the policy right out the window. Where is the new Liberal party? Where is the nationalism and the concern for Canada's energy security? It is gone.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: It was never there.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: They fooled you.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
We asked questions in the House with respect to whether there were any swap provisions in this agreement. Swap provisions are very simple and can easily be understood
Alaska Gas Pipeline
by Canadians. That is, if we intend to sell off all this gas now, let us make a deal with the United States that we receive some of that Alaska gas when it comes down. But there are no swap provisions. The minister said as recently as last week that he was still negotiating with the American secretary of the interior, but there are no swap provisions and there are no guarantees.
Look at the guarantees. First of all, we have a resolution of the Congress. The minister knows and members know that one Congress does not bind another. Hon. members know Congress does not commit one cent to construction and that it is the private companies that build the pipelines, not the American Congress, and they are not going to guarantee it.
The second thing is that there is a letter from the President: "Dear Marc, Go ahead. Signed, Jimmy." What is this letter worth? I say with respect to the President, what is this letter worth, Madam Speaker? It is not committing Congress or the administration to one penny. It is certainly not committing any President afterwards. Does the government call this "guarantees"?
The third guarantee is that the pipeline companies, the oil companies, have spent some money; they have spent 2 per cent. On projects? No, on studies in Alaska.
Those are the ironclad guarantees, Madam Speaker. Those are what the minister comes to the House with tonight. He says they are jobs. They are jobs for one-tenth of the project. The project is going to cost about $600 million and upwards in Canada, plus the spin-off benefits. The whole line in Canada would cost $8 billion and the total line would cost $22 billion. Why should Canadian workers settle for one-tenth of the loaf when they can have the whole loaf? That does not make any sense. No, Madam Speaker, on this side of the House we think that line will never be build.
There is another matter at issue here but before I deal with it I heard something from my friends to my right. What is the position of the Conservative party on this? They are in favour of the pre-build.

speechtext: Cabinet dictatorship.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
We have asked for a debate in Parliament. We have asked for an amendment to this act-this act which may be illegal. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House the other day, "We are just building this northern pipeline by stages like you build the St. Lawrence Seaway- one lock at a time." The problem is that it is more like authorizing the building of the St. Lawrence Seaway and then building the Erie canal! It is totally different. It is comparing apples with oranges.
This is a very fundamental matter for Parliament, if we take Parliament seriously. Parliament authorized a transportation pipeline and then the government-not by coming back to Parliament but by order in council-authorizes an export pipeline. I hear it said that Parliament does not matter any more, that it is useless, that in this new age what we have is really cabinet dictatorship between elections.
It is up to us. Madam Speaker, to decide if we are going to let Parliament not matter any more. This is a fundamental issue that we in the NDP are going to continue fighting for.
At the conclusion of his remarkable speech when he was urging the building of a Canadian transcontinental railway, Sir John A. Macdonald, as reported at page 494 of Hansard, volume one, of the debate of 1880-81 said this:
"I can trust to the intelligence of this House, and the patriotism of this country. I can trust not only to the patriotism but to the common sense of this country to carry out an arrangement which will give us all we want, which will satisfy all the loyal, legitimate aspirations, which will give us a great, an united, a rich, an
improving, a developing Canada, instead of making us tributary to American laws, to American (gas companies) to American bondage, to American tolls, to American freights, to all the little tricks and big tricks that American (gas companies) arc addicted to-"
I have changed two of Sir John's words, Madam Speaker. In two places I changed the word "railway" to "gas companies". Otherwise that is a verbatim statement of Sir John A. Macdonald in this House in discussing the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I did that purposely, Madam Speaker, because in the Speech from the Throne the government said the same thing. They said that pipelines are really the railways of the twentieth century. I agree with that. That is why this matter is so important tonight. That is why we must not stuff this "railway" full of Canadian gas to go to the United States. That is why we must get rid of this colonial attitude or we will always remain a colony.
What we are doing is taking all our jobs and our gas and stuffing them into a pipeline and exporting them. That is the fundamental issue here. When hon. members opposite stand up and give the minister the kind of ovation they did, they should really think about that.

Up to the present time the government has ignored this. I cannot state emphatically enough that consideration must be given to this question.

The first one is the undertaking which we have been able to obtain in the United States between the producers and the distributors to commit $500 million for the engineering and the beginning of the work in Alaska; that is $500 million on the line.
Second, we have a letter from the President, on the interpretation of which I disagree strongly with my hon. friend. The president indicated a very strong commitment of the administration to the completion of this pipeline before the end of 1985.

He knows, or he should know, that there are only two parties in the United States, and after the election there will be either a Republican majority or a Democratic majority in the Congress. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. minister can tell the House whether, in his opinion, this decision concerning the Alaska pipeline construction will have an impact on the construction or the extension of the pipeline between Quebec and Montreal as concerns either the availability of materials, the question of financing or other construction delays. Could this affect or delay construction or could it even have favourable effects?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to inform my colleague, the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) that we do not believe that tonight's decision will have any unfavourable effect on the construction of the Quebec pipeline. On the contrary, the action we are taking will have the effect of phasing the construction of the Alaska pipeline over several years beginning immediately, and this will enable the steel companies and the pipeline material suppliers to schedule the production of steel and other products required for the pipeline operation over several years and prevent production hold-ups, which in general considerably increase the costs and sometimes even cause product shortages and can prevent the construction or the completion of other projects.
As for the construction of the Quebec pipeline, I have been informed recently that the Quebec government has asked

July 17, 1980

TransCanada PipeLines, which is not the same company as the one building the Alberta pipeline, once again to change the proposed route for the pipeline in Quebec. I must say that this decision worries me and that I am afraid it might substantially delay the construction of the Quebec pipeline. I hope that I am wrong.
1 also hope that the decision made by the Quebec government as concerns TransCanada PipeLines can be implemented very quickly, as we have already lost several very precious months because of the way the Quebec government has postponed essential decisions, and if this new decision delays even more the building of the pipeline, Quebeckers will be the ones to suffer. First of all, they will have to pay more for heating
oil.	They will be prevented form burning Canadian natural gas instead of oil and Quebec consumers are the ones who are and will be suffering from the way the Quebec government is delaying, exaggeratedly in my opinion, its decision in this matter.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just like to ask the minister a couple of questions. First, can he tell me what percentage of the natural gas that was approved for export to the United States in 1978 and 1979 was actually exported?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: The hon. member raises a very good question in the sense that at present the level of exports to the United States is well below the authorized level, so that when the hon. member talks about a large amount being exported he has to remember that these are authorized levels, they are not necessarily actual levels. I believe that at present, for instance in British Columbia, the percentage of exports is as low as 35 per cent of the authorized level. I might be wrong by a few percentage points, but it is in that area. So far as Alberta is concerned or so far as the average production is concerned, 1 think it is slightly above 50 per cent. I will inquire and give my friend the exact figure.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Fifty-eight per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: My knowledgeable friend from the Yukon says it is 58 per cent. In spite of his great expertise, I think I will inquire from my officials.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Can the minister tell me if any of the reasons for this gas not being exported have to do with the price of the natural gas?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
It is a combination of several factors. As the hon. member knows, we had an extremely mild winter last year which resulted in a level of consumption, both in Canada and in the United States, that was much lower than had been the case before.
Second, the United States has experienced a rather deep recession in the last year and a half, which is still continuing and which has resulted also in a lowering in the consumption of petroleum products generally, including natural gas.
Alaska Gas Pipeline
Third, there is obviously a particular problem in certain sections of the U.S., particularly the northwestern states where there is an oversupply of residual fuels being used for commercial and industrial purposes as a substitution for Canadian gas in particular. In effect, our gas at present sells for about $4.47 at the border. I am told that it is possible, in view of the situation with residual oil, to get the equivalent perhaps for about $4.07 or $4.10. So there is an advantage which we believe is temporary in favour of residual fuel in the northwest states of the United States. We are confident that this is a passing phenomenon and that with the increase in the cost of oil on the international market, and the expected resumption of activity in the U.S. economy, the demand for Canadian gas will soon pick up, particularly with an increase in the price of residual fuels.

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: In light of the minister's answer, I wonder if he could tell me if, in the discussions with his colleagues today, there was mention of a possibility of a tax on the export of natural gas.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: I apologize to the hon. member, but the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) was in a great conversation with me and I did not hear his question. Would he ask his question again?

subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Can the minister tell me if his colleagues discussed today the possibility of an export tax on natural gas?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always followed the policy of not only not revealing discussions in cabinet, but refusing to confirm or deny whether any question was discussed in cabinet. So I am afraid my hon. friend will have to look elsewhere for an answer.
To come back to his first question concerning the exact percentage of exports of natural gas, I do not have the exact figure tonight. I am told the average current level would be about 60 per cent. I am sorry I do not have exactly the same figure as the hon. member for Yukon.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: I was closer than you.

At the same time, may I inquire as to the status of the much talked about and proposed MEB, the Maritime Energy Board, as well as to the status and attitude of the various provinces within Atlantic Canada, particularly the province in which my constituency resides, New Brunswick. speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my information is to the effect that Atlantic Canada would benefit from this particular

July 17, 1980
Alaska Gas Pipeline
announcement, roughly to the extent of $10 million. With the construction of the whole line, it is estimated that an additional $200 million will go to Atlantic Canada, for a total of about $210 million for the line which will be constructed in Alberta, British Columbia and the Yukon. Certainly, that is not a negligible sum. As far as the second part of the question is concerned, I believe the hon. member was asking about the maritime pipeline.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: The Maritime Energy Board.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: The Maritime Energy Corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: 1 am afraid I have to report that at the present time this particular corporation is somewhat in limbo. There appear to be very conflicting views among the various maritime governments. 1 hope we will be able to get the situation back on the rails. In particular, I hope the provincial governments concerned will agree to sit down and work out an arrangement which would be beneficial to the entire mari-times. 1 am sorry to say that we have been unable to get this corporation going at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. For the benefit of the House and the residents of New Brunswick, does the minister anticipate, from the information he has to date, any difficulties or problems in terms of the eastern pipeline going from Quebec into New Brunswick and Atlantic Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: APPROVAL OF ALASKA GAS PIPELINE PRE-BUILD SECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated that the construction of a Montreal-Maritimes pipeline was the preferred and privileged option of the government. The National Energy Board has recommended the construction of the pipeline up to Quebec City first of all. We have authorized the implementation of this recommendation of the board, and that will imply the construction of the first phase of the maritime pipeline. Hopefully, the environmental concerns that were raised, the questions regarding the environmental studies and
certain reservations expressed in particular by New Brunswick, all this will be quickly settled. The NEB also indicated that it was interested in knowing more about the reserves found off Sable Island. I must add that the government is following the situation very closely and we want to make sure that the pipeline gets under way as quickly as possible. In the meantime, as I have indicated, the decision we have announced tonight and the eventual construction of the Alaska pipeline will represent benefits of almost $200 million for the Atlantic provinces.
Very shortly then when we build the pipeline to Quebec City and obviously also to the maritimes, I am sure that businesses and workers in the Atlantic provinces will derive substantial benefits from this decision, as well as all consumers in the maritimes.
